name: authors-api-concurrency
description: API, concurrency and code design principles. Design and implementation scope, so they fire only on sections that describe interfaces or concurrency. No text reused.

rules.title: Public interfaces are minimal and hard to misuse
rules.requirement: The interface exposes only what callers need, defaults are safe, invalid states are unrepresentable where practical, and the design says which parts are stable contract and which are not.

source.name: Joshua Bloch
source.locator: How to Design a Good API and Why it Matters, 2006 talk; Effective Java, 3rd ed.

rules.title: Compatibility rules for the interface are stated
rules.requirement: The design says what counts as a breaking change, how versions are signalled, how long old versions are supported, and how deprecation is communicated.

source.name: Joshua Bloch
source.locator: Effective Java, 3rd ed., Item 15 and API design talk, compatibility

rules.title: Errors fail fast with actionable detail and no leakage
rules.requirement: The interface reports invalid input immediately, error responses say what went wrong in terms the caller can act on, and never expose internals such as stack traces or secrets.

source.name: Joshua Bloch
source.locator: Effective Java, 3rd ed., Item 49, Check parameters for validity

rules.title: Shared mutable state is confined or immutable
rules.requirement: The design names what state is shared between threads or workers, and for each either confines it to one owner, makes it immutable, or names the synchronisation that guards it.

source.name: Brian Goetz with Tim Peierls
source.locator: Java Concurrency in Practice, Chapters 2 and 3

rules.title: Thread pools and queues are bounded and sized with a reason
rules.requirement: Each executor or worker pool has a stated size with the reasoning behind it, a bounded work queue, and a named rejection policy when the queue is full.

source.name: Brian Goetz and colleagues
source.locator: Java Concurrency in Practice, Chapter 8, Applying Thread Pools

rules.title: Blocking is avoided on the paths that must scale
rules.requirement: Request-serving paths do not block a scarce thread on I/O or on a lock held across a remote call. The design names the non-blocking or reactor style used, or shows that threads are plentiful enough for a blocking model.

source.name: Doug Lea
source.locator: Scalable IO in Java, 2003; Concurrent Programming in Java, 2nd ed.

rules.title: Locks have the smallest scope and a consistent order
rules.requirement: Where locks are used, each guards one clearly named invariant, is held for the shortest time, never across a remote call, and locks taken together are taken in one documented order.

source.name: Doug Lea
source.locator: Concurrent Programming in Java, 2nd ed., Chapter 2, Exclusion

rules.title: Simplicity, robustness and portability are stated design goals
rules.question: Where in this design did you choose simplicity over cleverness, and where did you choose portability over a platform-specific feature? Name one of each.

source.name: James Gosling
source.locator: The Java Language Environment white paper, 1996, design goals
